paras: The Caperton Station shooting was the shooting of a Black striking miner named Lewis by J. W. St. Clair, the prosecuting attorney of Fayette County, West Virginia, at Caperton Station on the evening of November 1, 1881. St. Clair fired on Lewis as he tried to escape after his arrest, and the first dispatches reported him killed. Later reports said he had only been wounded, and one Washington paper questioned whether he had been shot for striking or for being Black.

Lewis was described as one of the leaders of a strike at the Caperton mines in Fayette County, which the Kanawha Gazette called the works of Cooper & Co. According to the Gazette, he had committed "some offense against the law," and a warrant was issued for his arrest.

St. Clair accompanied the constable who made the arrest. A Virginia weekly reported that the prisoner was held in the depot at Caperton Station and tried to escape when he was brought out to be put on the train. As he ran, St. Clair fired five shots at him, three of which hit him. All accounts of how the shooting happened come from the officers' side.

No report of an inquest or of any charge against St. Clair appears in the coverage. In December, St. Clair told a Wheeling Register correspondent in Washington that on "the day I shot the negro who was endeavoring to escape" he had been threatened by a mob, and that he had received some twenty anonymous letters threatening his life. In the same interview he argued that strikers had to be met with "Force With Force" and called for trespass legislation against the miners' union.

The first word came in a Charleston special dispatch to the Wheeling Intelligencer, headed "A Business Prosecutor," which reported that St. Clair had "shot and killed a negro named James Lewis." The same story ran on November 3 in the Memphis Daily Appeal under "An Obstreperous Miner Killed," naming the victim Joseph Lewis, and in the St. Paul Daily Globe's news roundup. These items gave the escape account as fact, and the Morgantown New Dominion reprinted it among its state clippings on November 12.

The Washington National Republican was the only paper found to question the killing. It noted that Lewis was charged with being "troublesome" and asked whether prosecutors there went "gunning for all striking miners" or whether he was "killed for being black." Closer to the scene, the Point Pleasant Weekly Register printed the Kanawha Gazette's fuller account on November 9 and a week later reported that "the negro only received a slight flesh wound."

The papers disagreed on whether Lewis died: the Charleston dispatch and the Kanawha Gazette said he was killed, while the Weekly Register's correction and the Stephens City Star said he was wounded, slightly or "severely." The later reports explicitly corrected the first ones, and St. Clair himself spoke in December only of having shot the man. His first name was given as Joseph, James and Lew, and the Gazette dated the shooting to "last Monday" rather than Tuesday evening.

The shooting itself is reported independently by a Charleston dispatch and the Kanawha Gazette (A4, A7), but the first reports that Lewis was killed (A1, A4, A7) are contradicted by later West Virginia and Virginia reports that he was only wounded (A9, A10).

accounts.label: Charleston wire dispatch
accounts.gist: St. Clair shot and killed Lewis, a strike leader, who made an effort to escape while under arrest.

accounts.label: Kanawha Gazette
accounts.gist: A warrant was issued for Lewis for some offense; on the way back after the arrest he broke away and ran, and St. Clair fired five shots, three taking effect, killing him.

accounts.label: Later corrections
accounts.gist: Lewis was not killed: one paper said he received only a slight flesh wound, another that he was severely wounded when he tried to escape as he was brought from the depot to the train.

accounts.label: St. Clair's own statement
accounts.gist: He shot 'the negro who was endeavoring to escape' and was threatened by a mob that day.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal and Wheeling Intelligencer ran the escape account as fact under 'An Obstreperous Miner Killed' and 'A Business Prosecutor'.
The National Republican asked whether public prosecutors 'go gunning for all striking miners' or whether Lewis was killed 'for being black as well as "troublesome"'.
West Virginia weeklies reprinted the Kanawha Gazette's fuller account and then corrected the death report without comment.
In a Wheeling Register interview St. Clair defended meeting strikers with 'Force With Force' and presented the shooting as stopping an escape.

conflicts.note: No paper names a second victim; the later reports do not name him (A9, A10).

The later reports are explicit corrections or a fuller later account from the region, so they are better evidence than the first dispatches; St. Clair's own December statement says only that he 'shot' the man (A11).
The Nov. 2 dispatches are closest to the event; a Nov. 26 Virginia weekly also says 'Tuesday evening' (A10).
Both place it in Fayette County; the shooting took place at Caperton Station (A10).
